description: History as a set of eras, each opened up into the ideas that defined it, with the Renaissance as the deepest branch.

concepts.title: History
concepts.summary: The record of what people did and why we think they did it. It's never quite the past itself, only the part someone wrote down and someone else chose to read, and it's always being revised.

concepts.title: Prehistory
concepts.summary: Everything before writing, which is nearly all of the human story. We read it in bones, stone tools, and pigment on cave walls, and we know it far less well than we'd like.

concepts.title: Fire
concepts.wiki: Control of fire by early humans
concepts.summary: Tamed at least hundreds of thousands of years ago. It cooked food, kept the dark and cold at bay, and gave people an evening: a reason to gather and talk once the light was gone.

concepts.title: Cave Art
concepts.summary: Animals and hands in ochre on deep cave walls, some more than forty thousand years old. Whoever made them had already learned to picture what wasn't there.

concepts.title: Ancient World
concepts.summary: The first farms, cities, writing, and empires, growing up along rivers from Mesopotamia and Egypt to India and China. Nearly every institution we know started to take shape here.

concepts.title: Agriculture
concepts.summary: Around ten thousand years ago people began to plant instead of only gather. It fed far more of them, tied them to a place, and set the stage for cities, property, and kings.

concepts.title: Cities
concepts.summary: Places where thousands of strangers live close together. They concentrate trade, ideas, and disease, and they need laws, food supply, and shared stories to hold together.

concepts.title: Empires
concepts.summary: One power ruling many peoples. They spread roads, languages, and taxes, and they sooner or later strain under their own size, and their rise and fall shaped the map more than almost anything.

concepts.title: Ancient Greece
concepts.summary: A scatter of small, quarrelsome city-states that argued its way into philosophy, geometry, drama, and democracy. What they left is less a set of answers than a habit of asking why.

concepts.title: Ancient Rome
concepts.summary: A city that became a republic, then an empire spanning the Mediterranean. Its engineering, law, and Latin outlasted it by more than a thousand years.

concepts.title: Ancient Egypt
concepts.summary: A civilization that grew along the Nile and lasted three thousand years. It built with stone on a scale that still astonishes and cared deeply about death and its order.

concepts.title: Middle Ages
concepts.summary: The long stretch after Rome fell in the west. The label was invented later, and it hides how much happened: monasteries, universities, new trade routes, and thriving cultures far beyond Europe.

concepts.title: The Silk Road
concepts.summary: A web of trade routes across Asia that carried silk, spices, paper, religions, and diseases between East and West. Ideas traveled as steadily as goods.

concepts.title: Islamic Golden Age
concepts.summary: From about the eighth century, scholars in Baghdad and beyond translated, preserved, and extended Greek, Persian, and Indian learning. Algebra, optics, and medicine advanced, and the knowledge later reached Europe.

concepts.title: The Black Death
concepts.summary: A plague that swept Eurasia in the fourteenth century and killed a large share of the people in its path. It left labor scarce, wages higher, and old certainties shaken.

concepts.title: Feudalism
concepts.summary: A web of obligations in which land was held in return for service, protection, and loyalty. Historians debate how tidy it ever was, but it shaped who owed what to whom for centuries.

concepts.title: Universities
concepts.summary: Guilds of students and teachers that took shape in medieval Europe. They gave learning a home, a curriculum, and a degree, and they are one of the few institutions from that time still going.

concepts.title: The Renaissance
concepts.summary: A rebirth of interest in the ancient world that began in Italian cities and spread across Europe. It fused art, science, money, and a new confidence in the individual, and it changed how people saw.

concepts.title: Humanism
concepts.summary: A movement that put human questions and the study of classical writers at the center of education. It asked what a person could become, and treated learning as a way to become it.

concepts.title: Perspective
concepts.summary: A geometric method for drawing three-dimensional space on a flat surface, worked out in fifteenth-century Florence. Lines converge at a vanishing point, and painting suddenly looked like a window.

concepts.title: Printing Press
concepts.summary: Gutenberg's movable type made books cheap enough to own. Ideas spread faster than any authority could manage, and reading, argument, and standardized languages followed.

concepts.title: The Medici
concepts.summary: A Florentine banking family whose money and patronage paid for much of Renaissance art and learning. It is a reminder that culture is often funded by commerce, for mixed motives.

concepts.title: Leonardo
concepts.summary: Painter, anatomist, engineer, and endlessly curious observer, whose notebooks mix flying machines with studies of water and the human heart. He treated seeing as a kind of thinking.

concepts.title: Age of Discovery
concepts.summary: European voyages around Africa and across the Atlantic joined the world's oceans, and with them plants, animals, ideas, and diseases. The exchange enriched some and devastated many.

concepts.title: Enlightenment
concepts.summary: A seventeenth- and eighteenth-century push to use reason, evidence, and open debate instead of inherited authority. It gave us modern science, rights, and its own blind spots.

concepts.title: Scientific Revolution
concepts.summary: Copernicus, Galileo, Newton: the Earth moves, motion has laws, and mathematics is the language of nature. Method and measurement replaced quoting the ancients.

concepts.title: Democracy
concepts.summary: Rule by the people, in some form. Athens tried it first and it was revived in modern shapes, and it always turns out to be less a finished system than an ongoing, argumentative practice.

concepts.title: The Encyclopédie
concepts.summary: A vast French project of the mid-1700s to gather all human knowledge in one work, arranged for anyone to read. Its ambition, to make knowledge shared and searchable, is a distant ancestor of Wikipedia.

concepts.title: Industrial Revolution
concepts.summary: From around 1760, coal and steam moved work from hands to machines. Output soared and cities swelled, and it changed how people lived faster than any change before it.

concepts.title: Factories
concepts.summary: Machines, workers, and a clock in one building. Division of labor multiplied what a person could make and changed the rhythm of a day from the sun's to the shift's.

concepts.title: Urbanization
concepts.summary: People moving to cities for work. For the first time in history, more of humanity lives in cities than outside them, and the shift is still underway.

concepts.title: Capitalism
concepts.summary: An economic system where private owners invest to make profit and prices coordinate the rest. It has produced enormous wealth and equally enormous arguments about who gets to share it.

concepts.title: Information Age
concepts.summary: From the mid-twentieth century, computers and networks made information the main thing being made, moved, and fought over. The change is recent enough that we're still inside it.

concepts.title: Globalization
concepts.summary: Trade, money, people, and ideas moving across borders faster and in greater volume. It linked distant lives together, and it is why a single supply chain can span a dozen countries.

concepts.title: Mass Media
concepts.summary: Print, radio, television, and now the web: channels that reach millions at once. Whoever controls them shapes what a society pays attention to.
